schools.summary: Gill argues 'the day' marks a season, not the day the tabernacle was first reared; Calvin holds the princes gave in their tribes' name, and that Moses' unanointed hand proves the virtue of consecration is not the man's.

Wesley lays out the sequence of events that fixes the time and notes the offerings kept the order of the encampment; Clarke dates it to the second day of the second month and would place the account after Leviticus 10.
Henry takes the timing as a rule — necessary observances before free-will offerings — and the princes' precedence as what rank is for.

debates.question: What day is 'the day that Moses had fully set up the tabernacle'?

sides.position: not one particular day but the season, since the offerings ran twelve days
the second day of the second month of the second year, the account belonging after Leviticus 10

outliers.note: Presses that Moses, himself unanointed, anointed both sanctuary and priest — so the efficacy of consecration cannot have come from him.

2.pericope_label: Six covered wagons and twelve oxen brought before the LORD

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch weigh the versions on the disputed word — covered wagons against the Septuagint's lampenic vehicles — and reject 'litters' on etymological grounds.
Clarke grants nobody knows what a lampenic chariot was and settles for 'covered' or 'tilted'; Wesley reads the wagons as provision for the more cumbersome parts.

Calvin argues the covering was against rain, cites Ainsworth on the tortoise-shell etymology, and refuses any difference between 'before the LORD' and 'before the tabernacle'; Gill locates the presentation at the tabernacle where God had taken up his habitation.
Henry notes provision for removal was made the moment the tabernacle was settled, and that the wagons were accepted though no pattern of them was shown in the mount.

debates.question: What kind of vehicle were the six wagons?

sides.position: covered or tilted wagons, for carrying the tabernacle's materials

holders: Gesenius (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
De Wette (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Eusebius of Emesa (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

4.pericope_label: The LORD commands Moses to receive the gift and divide it by service

schools.summary: Gill reads 'take it of them' as God's verdict that the freewill offering was of his own prompting and acceptable; Calvin renders the following clause as a pluperfect, making the tribute required before it was brought.
Keil and Delitzsch gloss 'to every man according to his service' as distribution to the classes of Levites in the measure their duties required.
Clarke and Wesley both read the rule as need rather than equality — most to those with the heaviest burdens, more or fewer as the things carried required.

debates.question: Was the command to receive the wagons given before or after the princes presented them?

sides.position: before — read as a pluperfect, God had required this tribute of the people
after — 'the LORD said unto Moses' when the gift was already presented

6.pericope_label: Moses divides the wagons: Gershon, Merari, and none for Kohath

schools.summary: Clarke explains each share from what the family carried and holds sacred things must not be drawn by beasts; Wesley grounds the Kohathites' shoulders in the greater holiness of their charge.
Keil and Delitzsch add that Merari's service was under the hand of Ithamar and that the holy things had poles provided for shoulder-carriage.
Henry weighs the silver sockets at over four tons, infers the Merarites shouldered them, and reads the whole division as strength proportioned to work.
Gill notes Moses took the wagons as directed and that Merari received all that remained.

outliers.note: Points forward to Uzza: when David's men carried the ark in a cart they learned to their terror that they had not sought the Lord in the due order.

10.pericope_label: The dedication of the altar, one prince to a day

schools.summary: Gill sets the dedication after the anointing and notes Moses did not know the manner of offering till God fixed it; Calvin assigns dish, bowl and censer their uses, works at the shekel's value, and leaves the gold shekel undecided.
Henry calls the altars handselled by the princes, itemises the silver and gold by weight and use, and argues Israel could afford it, being fed from heaven and shortly to possess Canaan.
Wesley distinguishes this from the first consecration by Moses and Aaron; Clarke notes each prince offered on behalf and at the expense of his tribe.
Keil and Delitzsch state that the order of presentation followed the order of the tribes in the camp.

outliers.note: Thinks the spreading of the gifts over twelve days was itself devotional — a lengthened exercise to stir up careless hearts.

12.pericope_label: The first day: Nahshon of Judah offers

schools.summary: Calvin hears Jacob's oracle on the sceptre behind Judah's precedence and reads the first day as a presage of David's kingdom; Gill gives the plainer reason, that Judah's standard was pitched first on the east, and prices the golden spoon.
Henry notes Nahshon alone is not called a prince, prefers the reading that the title belonged more properly to Christ, and sets Judah first as the firstfruits are first.
Clarke identifies charger, bowl and spoon as kneading dish, blood basin and censer; Wesley keeps the charger out of the sanctuary and explains why the peace offerings are the most numerous.

debates.question: Why is Nahshon alone not called a prince?

sides.position: so that the man who offered first should not be puffed up, the rest being titled because they submitted and followed
holders: the Jewish explanation reported by Henry

sides.position: because the title prince of Judah belonged more properly to Christ

themes: every kind of offering at once

18.pericope_label: The second day: Nethaneel of Issachar offers

schools.summary: Clarke observes the princes come forward in exactly the order in which their tribes were encamped about the tabernacle.
Keil and Delitzsch read the sequence the same way, from Judah's prince first to Naphtali's last.

fidelity.note: Carried by Clarke's camp-order table at v14 and Keil and Delitzsch at v11; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

24.pericope_label: The third day: Eliab of Zebulun offers

schools.summary: Calvin explains why Zebulun and Issachar are ranked under Judah's banner: they were Leah's two youngest sons, following next after Judah her fourth.

fidelity.note: Carried by Calvin's block at v12 on Judah's banner; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

30.pericope_label: The fourth day: Elizur of Reuben offers

schools.summary: Calvin answers the objection that Reuben the firstborn is kept back: the fourth day heads the second division, and to lead three tribes is the more honourable place.

themes: the same gift from every tribe

fidelity.note: Carried by Calvin's block at v12 on the four divisions; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

36.pericope_label: The fifth day: Shelumiel of Simeon offers

schools.summary: Henry takes the identical offerings as a deliberate sign that every tribe had an equal share in the altar and an equal interest in its sacrifices, and applies it against respect of persons.

fidelity.note: Carried by Henry's block at v10 on the identical offerings; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

42.pericope_label: The sixth day: Eliasaph of Gad offers

schools.summary: Henry asks why identical gifts are recorded at length twelve times, and answers that no tribe might seem slighted and that God records every gift with its giver's name.

fidelity.note: Carried by Henry's block at v10 on why the record repeats; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

48.pericope_label: The seventh day: Elishama of Ephraim offers

schools.summary: Clarke answers the objection that the seventh day fell on a sabbath: it is not proved that it did, and no day could be too holy for acts that were all religious acts.
Henry judges that a sabbath must have fallen within the twelve days and that they did not break off for it, this being holy work.

themes: holy work on a holy day

54.pericope_label: The eighth day: Gamaliel of Manasseh offers

schools.summary: Clarke reads the uniform quantity as an equal debt equally acknowledged, and the sacrificial vessels and clean animals as marking out a people wholly dedicated to God.

fidelity.note: Carried by Clarke's block at v14 on equal debt and clean animals; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

60.pericope_label: The ninth day: Abidan of Benjamin offers

schools.summary: Clarke closes his account of the gifts with Ainsworth's reading: the sacrifices of all sorts figure the death of Christ and the benefits received by it.

outliers.note: Reads the completeness of the list christologically — reconciliation, dedication and communion in one day's gift.

fidelity.note: Carried by Clarke's Ainsworth quotation at v14; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

66.pericope_label: The tenth day: Ahiezer of Dan offers

schools.summary: Henry fastens on the sin offering standing in the middle of a festival, and reads it as repentance mixed into our most joyful services, with an eye to Christ the great sin offering.

fidelity.note: Carried by Henry's block at v10 on the sin offering amid joy; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

72.pericope_label: The eleventh day: Pagiel of Asher offers

schools.summary: Clarke unfolds the Hebrew idiom for 'the eleventh day' — in the day, the first and tenth day — and turns the oddity back on the English words eleven and twelve, calling the whole a matter of philology.
Gill enters the prince with his father and his tribe as the record has it.

78.pericope_label: The twelfth day: Ahira of Naphtali offers

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch close the sequence where the camp's order closes it, with the prince of Naphtali last.
Clarke notes the Hebrew counts the twelfth day as it counted the eleventh.

Henry gathers the reasons for spreading the gifts over twelve days: the solemnity prolonged and remembered, equal honour to each tribe, order rather than hurry, the priests' hands set in, and peace offerings that had to be eaten the same day.

themes: a day apiece, a stone apiece

fidelity.note: Carried by Henry at v10, Keil and Delitzsch at v11 and Clarke at v72; faithful to the chapter's catena, not to the span's own slot.

schools.summary: Clarke reads 'in the day when it was anointed' as pointing to the twelfth and last day, and 'after that it was anointed' as the note of consecration; Wesley reads the same phrase as the chapter correcting itself, the dedication following the anointing in a latitude.
Gill works through the totals — the spoons' use, the twelve bullocks answering to the twelve princes, the twenty-four at two apiece.

Gill takes the voice for the Shechinah, the eternal Word, not the Father's, which no man has heard; Calvin resolves the apparent clash with the cloud that once barred the door by dating Moses' access before Aaron's priesthood began.
Clarke derives the name debir, the speaking place, and makes the incarnate Christ the true oracle; Wesley reads the verse as God's answer once men had done their part.

debates.question: How could Moses enter, when a cloud once filled the door so that he could not?

sides.position: he sought God's replies at the mercy seat until Aaron began to exercise the priesthood, and the verse states what had been true throughout rather than what followed the offerings
the verse records what happened when Moses went in after the twelve days

themes: the voice from the mercy seat
